title: The Best Since 'Empire' - An Absolute Triumph in Film-making!
review:
I have to say, I was extremely enthusiastic about seeing this movie. I really like Star Wars, and this was supposedly the last film they'd ever have. It would tie up all the loose ends of the saga, and complete one of the most loved and successful movie sagas of all time. The whole ride over to the movie theater that was playing 'Revenge of the Sith', the Star Wars theme was playing in my head, and I was beyond anxious to see how good (or unfortunately, how bad) this film would be. I read good and bad reviews of the third episode of the Star Wars films, some said it was the best one since 'The Empire Strikes Back', and other said it was just a poorly written, loud and expensive peace of Hollywood junk. I had an idea I would enjoy the film, but I didn't know how much. After waiting in line for a half an hour, and sitting in the movie theater for forty-five minutes, those legendary opening credits started to roll, and the crowd started screaming and cheering in excitement. After the film was completed, I knew that this was the best Star Wars installment since 'The Empire Strikes Back', and maybe even better. 'Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith' is more then just a great movie, it's a triumph and a hell of a way to end a mind-boggling Sci-Fi saga. I loved it!

The third episode of the Star Wars film's story is very pessimistic in almost every way. It's the downfall of Anakin Skywalker (Hayden Christensen) as a good guy and his turn to the dark side and his eventual transformation into Darth Vader. Anakin is a good and honest jedi, but he's very arrogant and pompous. When he's invited to be a part of the jedi council but not made a master, it infuriates him and causes him to become distant from his trainer, Obi-Wan Kenobi (played masterfully, of course, by U.K. film actor Ewan McGregor), and become closer with the corrupt and evil, Supreme Chancellor Palpatine (Ian McDiarmid), who's secretly the Sith leader (the Jedi council's biggest enemy). Anakin slowly but surely becomes seduced by the dark side, and it effects his relationships with Obi-Wan and his secret wife and former Queen of Naboo, Padme (Natalie Portman - in a very different role then her's in 'Garden State'). George Lucas' latest Star Wars installment, definitely contains the most mind-boggling visuals and action sequences then any of the other Star Wars pictures, with another stand-out fight scene with Yoda kicking Sith butt, and a powerful and visually stunning lightsaber duel between Anakin and Obi-Wan over a river of hot lava.

Although the film's action and story line is truly genius, the film's acting is a little iffy. Ewan McGregor is outstanding as to be expected as the wise jedi master of Anakin, giving the best performance of the film. Natalie Portman is good as always as Padme, and McDiarmid and Samuel L. Jackson give first-rate performances in their roles. The real disappointment is Hayden Christensen. I could think of many actors who could play the role so much better then Christensen. The problem is Christensen isn't that good of an actor, he's very one-dimensional, and to play a character as confused, conflicted and complicated as Anakin Skywalker, you need to be a multi-dimensional actor. He never really made you believe he was going through harsh changes, and that kind of affected the film's greatness. Fortunatley, all the other undeniably wonderful aspects of the film almost make up for his lackluster and tiresome performance. George Lucas does a excellent job directing and writing this soon to be classic, and it's such an improvement of his work on both Episode I and II.

All in all, when everything is said and done, 'Revenge of the Sith' is an incredibly remarkable achievement in science fiction film-making. The reason why Star Wars is such a wonderful and well-received saga, is because the original 1977 film (now known as Episode IV - A New Hope) was such a stride and landmark in American cinema. The original Star Wars really changed the world of film-making forever, and not many people have forgotten that. In closing, 'Episode III' is not only such an important film because of it's extraordinary quality, but because it concludes the film series with the biggest cult following in history -- STAR WARS! Grade: A- (screened at AMC Deer Valley 30, Phoenix, Arizona, 5/22/05)

title: Finest of the saga.
review:
Star Wars hasn't been doing so well lately. Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones both went down as pretty awful, and caused fans to lose all faith in Lucas. But you'd better start believing again. Lucas has created another masterpiece, surpassing even Empire Strikes Back for terms of sheer greatness.

Nearly all of the problems with I & II are fixed for III. The acting is better. Ian McDiarmid does a fantastic job as Palpatine, using an increasing amount of menace and evil as the movie progresses, right up to the climax of his acting, his emergence as the Emperor. Hayden Christensen has finally nailed Anakin, he manages to pull off the evil of Vader as well as some confusion as he isn't sure which path to take. Ewan McGregor is having fun as Obi-Wan, and is fantastic at appearing betrayed by Anakin. The only real problem with the acting is the romance scenes, but they can be chalked up to Lucas's complete inability to write a love scene.

Speaking of the writing, it's not all that bad in this. The dialogue gets pretty lousy at points, but there's also a lot of good lines. Expect to see "Only a Sith deals in absolutes" on an anti-Bush bumper sticker sometime. One lousy line manages to be really funny, because hearing Yoda say "Not if anything to say about it, I have." is hilarious.

The CG is top notch, surpassing even the wild effects used in episodes I and II. Yoda looks perfect. He doesn't look fake, he actually looks better than his original puppet self. He moves with an odd jerkiness, but that's probably to emulate how the puppet moved. The droids, especially General Grievous, look fantastic. On a close-up of Grievous's face, you'll struggle and fail to find any obvious evidence that he's not real. The clone troopers look better than regular people in suits would, it's hard to tell when a Wookiee is CG or not, and the space battles look incredible. If they make episodes VII-IX, they would be completely photorealistic by the end.

The small flaws in this movie are countered by all that it does right. Incredible lightsaber battles, from Grievous's four lightsabers, to the Emperor and Yoda leaping about the Senate, to Anakin and Obi-Wan battling on top of lava. Some laugh-out-loud moments, mostly including R2-D2. Acting and dialogue leaps and bounds beyond episodes I and II. I really hope they go on and make VII-IX. Just as the magic is back, I don't want it to be gone.

title: Lucas not redeemed.
review:
I recognize that it's hard for me to be objective with the prequel episodes of Star Wars--I grew up with Episodes 4, 5, and 6, and they are the bar at which the new movies are compared. I realize that this bias is not entirely fair, but it's the way it is. Sequels are held to a different standard, because they are built upon earlier work, and they have an obligation to that material.

With this in mind, I will quickly agree with most of the current reviews that Revenge of the Sith is the best of the prequels. It's darker, it has a more relevant story, and it actually evokes some real emotion, beyond the rush of hearing the opening score.

Unfortunately, I don't see the present IMDb rating of 8.2, nor the heaps of praise for George Lucas, supposedly redeemed of his earlier transgressions with the franchise. Revenge of the Sith is still hobbled by weak-ass dialogue, sub-par CGI, and questionable plot structure. It does have some great moments, but it is far from a great movie.

The way I see it, if you're going to spend three movies chronicling the downfall of a pivotal character, make the final transformation CONVINCING beyond a shadow of a doubt. I think this movie fails in that regard, with Lucas once again spending more time on chase scenes and secondary lightsabre duels than on actual drama and character development.

Revenge of the Sith is okay. It's better than Phantom Menace, it's better than Attack of the Clones, but it doesn't have the weight or depth of the first trilogy, and I don't think anyone should suggest it's in the same ball park. Just because the story is "bringing balance" to the trilogies it doesn't make it good--it just brings it closer to the original material.

title: Mediocre, and quite disappointing.
review:
What an endeavor! The culmination of a six-movie plot in the making over 27 years.

Was it destined to disappoint ? I don't think so.

But something quite sad has happened to the quality of films written and directed by George Lucas. In 1973, he did "American Graffiti", and in 1977 he did "Star Wars: A New Hope".

(One of the best SciFi/Adventure films ever made, "The Empire Strikes Back", was written by Lucas, but directed by Irvin Kershner. Then came "Return of the Jedi", directed by Richard Marquand.)

Plenty has been said about what went wrong in the next two Star Wars films, both written and directed by Lucas. But they filled in some plot elements, introduced necessary characters, and were preparation work for this final connecting summary. In general, the poor reviews centered on the characters being a combination of non-credible, irritating, or flat, and also on editing, and pacing.

After seeing ROTS, you have to wonder why Lucas, with all his power, wealth, and connections, did not have someone review #1) the key plot element (SPOILER: transition of Anakin from good to evil), #2) the pacing, #3) the editing, and #4) How to direct believable characters.

ROTS. What an unusual, unfortunate, perhaps prophetic acronym.

OK - #4 is the director's job, but somehow he seems to have lost touch with it since his 1973 and 1977 successes.

The #1 plot element was simply not believable. BIG SPOILER ALERT: How can someone be so tormented by nightmares about the impending death of his beloved wife that the stress barely shows on him ? How can he buy into a whimsical concept of supernatural power that might give him the power of that death, and proceed to execute and murder all his comrades ? Next he proceeds to take on the role of a murderer, to the point of methodically and thoroughly murdering children he probably helped train in the peaceful ways of the Jedi ? ?

SPOILER: Why did he do this ? Out of love for his wife, and fear of losing her, with no real threat, from person or group, in sight. Hello - trying to prepare for the situation where one loved life might be in jeopardy, so you'll murder dozens of friends and allies ??? Just hoping that this power might work if the one life you believe you care about is threatened.

Sarcasm: The dark side made him did it. Yeah - right. (It's a good thing that dark side is in a galaxy far, far away. In our neighborhood, we don't have such a handy scapegoat.)

The MPAA review board was kind with their PG-13 rating. Lucas pushed it right to the limits.

As for my rating of 5 out of 10, I can defend it, and it's my scale. I give so much weight for each of the various elements of a film, based on its target audience, and certainly in comparison of other works. However, in this case, the bar is very high, due to how much money and time Lucas had,and how much power he had over the final product. It sure does not look like anyone was telling him how to do anything creatively in this film, and it shows.

My recommendations for better films in the ScFi/Adventure Family genre:

  • The Incredibles


  • The Abyss (Far better on many levels, but can be intense)


  • Independence Day (watch the DVD extra features, to see what an editor is supposed to do: cut unneeded scenes, characters, elements.)


  • Willow (A LucasFilm, directed by Ron Howard.)


  • Pirates of the Caribbian (I know - not technically SciFi)


  • Raiders of the Lost Ark (written by Lucas, but directed by Spielberg)


  • If you want a wild ride for action and adventure, and don't mind a character that is evil enough to terrorize, try "Speed(1994)".


  • For sheer incredible special effects, see "Jurassic Park".


Anyone can make a list of worthwhile movies like this. There have been so many films that are better than ROTS. I'd recommend making your own list, and not expecting to put ROTS on it.

What a waste ! You will see fantastic cities, air-ships, creatures, machines, and sets fly by at a staggering rate. The attempt at pacing seems to involve expressionless dialog, although (SPOILERS) Senator Palpatine seemed to have the most depth to him. Whatever depth the Anakin character had got thrown away, and translated into blind rage.

title: Greatest Action/ Romance Movie seen in years
review: I have been a big Star Wars film for awhile, and I have enjoyed Episodes One and Two but both were missing something big; the heart of the film. Even if you don't like star wars, this film cant be missed.
