title: Boring people doing uninvolving things
review:
I notice from the voting breakdown that 47% of voters gave "Revenge of the Anagram" a full 10 points. Sad. I suppose that's what happens when you give 15 year olds the vote. Based on Yoda's dialogue alone the film would rate a 2 at best and Yoda's advice about emotional connection to Anakin was just a dreadful piece of pseudo-profound nonsense. The Wookies made more sense.

And the word "younglings". Just embarrassing.

That I gave this film 4 is based purely on the visuals. As so often happens, the technical guys came through in a big way while just about every other aspect of the film made their effort pointless. More proof, if we need it, that great special effects don't make a great film.

The reality is that the last three films have been a spectacular waste of resources, still leaving "Empire" as the Star Wars high water mark. The film George Lucas had least to do with is by far and away the best film in the series. And no amount of voting 10 for a dull piece of technical eye candy is going to change that.

title: Holding out for the Special Edition...
review:
With a day to think it over, all I can say is (pardon my Yodaspeak)... disappointed I am. Weak plot with more holes than a ten pound block of Swiss cheese. Wooden characters, no humor, dialog ranging from forgettable to embarrassing. The best line had to be when Anakin lops off Dooku's hands and then manages to keep a straight face while spouting off "I shouldn't kill him - he's unarmed". Ya he's unarmed - you just cut his flippin' hands off! Was this Lucas' lame attempt to interject a James Bond-esqe one-liner? More likely, Lucas is just too out of it to make the connection, and nobody on the set cared enough to point it out to the big guy. Whatever you say GeorgeYou da man.

I can't help think about all the wasted potential. In the original Star Wars, didn't Obi Won tell us that the Jedi were hunted down and slaughtered by Vader himself. They could have done the Vader transformation early on, then made this the focus of the second half of the movie. We'd all rather Darth Vader getting' his bad groove on, than another hour of that whiny Hayden Christianson. They also could have done more to set up the rising rebellion and the motivation behind building the Death Star. At least it would have been a hell of lot better than showing him slaughtering a bunch of children. Vader the child-killer - are we ever supposed to feel sympathy for him after that? And that whole defection to the dark side - it took like two freakin' minutes. My wife thought it would have at least been cool if they showed the Emperor using some sort of dark magic to place those dreams in Anakin's mind. Good grief, even a non-Star Wars fan like her can cook up a better storyline than Lucas.

The only glimmer of hope I can see is the possibility that Lucas' fondness for tinkering with his films may eventually save the day. If he could somehow manage to isolate the good stuff from the first three films, cut out the bad (i.e. JarJar and half the talking robots), and then intersperse it with massive new dialog and plot changes there might still be some path to redemption. This would of course require tinkering on a scale never before seen on a major movie. He'd probably have to shoot many new scenes, use cutting edge CGI to morph new dialog over the faces of the actors. Perhaps the biggest hurdle though would be for Lucas himself to admit the first three movies were hobbled mainly by his poor writing and directing. He'd need to swallow his pride and bring on board a creative team with the firepower to bring his life's masterwork back from the abyss.

In many ways, Lucas' work has paralleled the Vader story itself. He started out looking like some sort of prodigy. Truly "A New Hope" for the Science Fiction genre. When he showed the good judgment and humility to step aside and let Irvin Kirshner take the reigns for Empire Strikes Back, he took his work to yet another level. At this point he was like a Jedi student learning from a master. By Return of the Jedi though the dark forces of cutesy marketing and unbridled special effects started taking hold. By the prequels, he'd fully cast aside most of what made him great in favor of blind focus on these false hopes. Like Vader, I'm sure he believes he's doing right, but in fact he's gone terribly wrong. Hopefully though like Anikin he'll eventually see the error in his ways and come back to the side of good. George Lucas - May the Force be with you.

Rich

title: Episode III just showed how good EP IV-VI was
review:
Yes, basically I have endured all 3 movies (ep I-III) just because the classic trilogy was THAT good. We all hoped for the genius to come back to Star Wars and when I have read the remarkable comments on EP III, I had hopes for the new trilogy.

But I was so wrong.

EP III lacks one thing: Emotions The ingredients were awesome, brave warriors, great love, treachery, a friendship that was more like 2 brothers, but the result was bad. I did not live with the characters in one single scene. Padme dies, no biggie, Anakin turned over to the dark side... I did not care, all Jedis died, I felt the urge to empty my bladder.

I did not believe that Anakin and Padme loved each other, I did not believe the reasons for Anakins turn that Lucas gave us, I did not feel for Obi Wan who had to battle his old friend.

In fact, I was watching the stunning special effects and the action, but not at the characters. As a result, my 2 favorite characters were Joda and R2-D2... one was CGI and the other a robot who cannot even speak. The movie was not bad, but take away the Star Wars feeling and the really big budget and you have a movie that could be Riddick 2.

George Lucas, you failed and I am sad because a great opportunity is missed. It was a nice history lesson, but like my history lessons in school, I was in danger of falling asleep the whole time.

Yes there are many fanboys who like this movie, but in 20 years, no one is going to speak of Ep I-III, the people will still watch the classic trilogy.

title: I wanted to love this but I was disappointed
review:
Before seeing this I was really excited. I saw 2 of the originals in the cinema as a child, Return of the Jedi as a treat for my first communion. ALONG time ago. And I LOVED them!! So onto ROTS, Why didn't I like it?

I hadn't unrealistic expectations, I knew it would be more in the mold of the first and second episodes, than 4-6.

Firstly it was supposed to be dark, and sure it was darker than the others, but I think Lucas really failed to deliver on the whole metamorphosis of Anaken to Darth Vader. It was all too easy!! You never really got a sense of his personal turmoil. If he really was this great Jedi knight, I would have expected WAY more internal conflict. a lot of this I'm afraid falls on the shoulders of Hadyn Christain, he was very poorly miscast, and doesn't have the presence for those crux moments when he NEEDS to deliver so much, and just can't.

Some of the acting was throwaway, wooden lines and cringe inducing one liners. But I could even have gotten over all that. I suppose I never felt excited during the film, there was no big rush and I guess a lot of that has to do with the fact that we already know the outcome.

Positives, I have utmost respect for McGregor, he was 90% excellent. He seemed to show much more personal conflict with Anakens destiny that Anaken ever did. I even really enjoyed Yoda, though again, should his Jedi powers not be stronger? A lot of the CGI was awesome, but again during the key scenes the volcanic fire etc, it looked like a playstation game. After epics like LOTR this fells second rate.

There was some good drama too, you couldn't but feel for Anaken, his whole life was tragic, he was played and conned, and only when it was too late do we really sense any regret.

But I was so disappointed in the creation of Darth Vader. I was expecting more mystique, a better explanation, I don't know the whole thing sort of feels very hollow to me now! In a way the whole illusion has been destroyed somewhat. I don't mean to be this harsh I'm just bitterly disappointed. Everyone says this is the film the fans wanted, do people genuinely think that was a great movie? Or do they feel compelled to say so out of loyalty to Lucas? Mmmmmmmm Hand on Heart I wish I loved it more!!

title: Best of I - III, but...
review:
'Sith' is easily the best of episodes I - III, but none of them belong anywhere near the same class as IV - VI. I enjoyed 'Sith,' but I have the following criticisms:

1. Acting. There wasn't any. In all three recent movies (Episodes I - III) the characters have NO personality. Everyone, even veteran actors Liam Neeson and Samuel L. Jackson, was wooden, wooden, wooden. I can't think of any character in episodes IV - VI who were so poor. I remember, following each of the first 3 movies, people were quoting memorable lines all over the place. Remember "What an incredible smell you've discovered!" or "Laugh it up, fuzzball?" There has been none of that from these three. In the new movies there is no banter, no humor, no personality. The one exception is Jar Jar Binks, but so many people found him annoying. I said at the time that I thought this was because he was the only character with personality in the movie. He stood out TOO much.

2. Over-dependence on computer animation. IV - VI were far more realistic-looking, because they made the effort to make it look that way.

I give episodes I - III each a 'C.' 'Sith,' maybe a C+.

title: better but not good enough
review:
WAY too much CGI, Lucas! After watching the new film, I reviewed The Empire Strikes back, easily the best of the bunch. That movie still looks wonderful and has the best story. The first two films appealed to the child's imagination in every audience member, the more recent trilogy appeals to a video game generation with a short attention span

I did appreciate Revenge of the Sith's Bush bashing though! There has never been a time of more evil in America than during Bush the second's reign, and I'm pleased that Lucas included his Bush criticism in what could easily have been a light as air adventure. Bush deserves to be bashed a lot more than this, but its a step in the right direction.

title: The best of the prequels
review:
I went to Revenge of the Sith not really knowing what to expect. Everybody I know that had seen it was giving me mixed reviews. Some thought that it was terrible, while others said it was one of the best Star Wars movies ever.

It definitely was not better then the original three but it was a very entertaining movie. The special effects and fight scenes were good but the film lacked a good script. Even proved good actors such as Ewan Magregor seemed bad. Hayden Christiansen seems to have little or no acting talent. With the faults aside, Geoge Lucas has made a good film and Revenge of the Sith is a success and is worth going to the theater to see. It is also definitely better then The Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones.

title: The Best Of The Prequels
review:
May Contain Spoilers! After the Phantom Menace & Attack Of The Clones (Fell asleep 2nd time I watched in cinema), I was looking forward to Revenge Of The Sith with more than a hint of concern. After IV, V & VI I wanted to see the conclusion of the story. I'm glad I did! A number of the story lines that link Attack & New Hope together are resolved. We all know that Anakin becomes Darth Vader. We all know Luke & Leia are Anakin's children.

One thing that does feel wrong. Leia said she remembers her mother just images but (SPOILER) Padme dies at the end of Revenge, so how can she remember her mother, unless she was never told that she was adopted and her adoptive mother died when Leia was young.

Again Lucas gives us an entertaining film with his story telling skills and laden with special effects from ILM (my fav special effects company). The fight scenes are great, light sabres galore. Yoda with his little LS is great in this film. R2D2 moves like he was on Fast Forward than in the other films.

I was very impressed with the amount of sets used, IV V & VI used only 3 per film, and General Grevious. We finally know the identity of Darth Sidious, as if we didn't know. But most surprising is how Master Windu dies, but who really kills him Sid or Annie. Could Windu survive if Annie hadn't cut off his arm.

Also Obi-Wan has a white LS not a Blue as he had in Phantom, I can't remember what he had in Attack, if he had a white or blue.

James Earl Jones is the voice of Vader again, but not credited in the end titles. Why? He was in IV, V & VI. Anyway I don't think that Hayden would do it as well as James, probably not menacing enough.

title: Darths and the Sith through all 6 films
review: Just curious to know if Lucas had the whole idea of there only being 2 Sith lords (one master, one apprentice) in mind when he made the first trilogy. At the end of ROTJ it's obvious the Emperor wants to discard Vader and take Luke on as his new apprentice, but in ESB, did Vader realize that this was the Emperor's intention? Actually, it was he who brought up the subject of converting Luke to the dark side during the hologram conversation with Palpatine. Perhaps they were both planning to betray each other. Or maybe the idea of there only being two Sith at a time hadn't yet solidified in Lucas's mind. I do find it strange that the word Sith is never mentioned in the last three films. And when Obi-Wan refers to Vader as Darth during their final fight, it seems odd that he would use that word instead of Vader or Anakin, considering Darth is more of a generic Sith title than a name.

title: A good script poorly executed.
review:
The good: Special effects are top notch! This movie delivers when it comes to excitement, and the storyline lives up to my expectations. There's a few very good 'movie moments' in this movie... the events following the issue of 'order 66' is bone-chilling.

The bad: Editing! At times the action moves so fast and the camera jumps around so quickly that one loses track of what's going on. Also, the scenes jump around a lot. Cut to two persons who each get to deliver one line, and off we go again to the next scene light years away. This was bad in Eps 1 and 2, but this movie takes it to new levels. The result is that we never really get the chance to get to know the characters, or build any sort of affection for them (or loathing as the case may be). Unlike Eps. 4 to 6, I did not find myself caring for any of the characters in this installment. Also, the staggering amount of locations and different creatures gets a bit overwhelming at times.

The ugly: Hayden Christensen's performance is very poor... 'wooden' does not even begin to describe it. At times when one would expect some genuine emotions to show, he delivers his lines in the same flat monotone.

On the whole, a good, very entertaining movie that (I expect) will not disappoint both new and old Star Wars fans. A shame about the jumbled editing and Christensen's performance; more attention to those areas would have made for a great movie instead of a good one.

title: Hack work - competently done, but no genius here.
review:
So, after the first trilogy was completed, what did George and the rest of us realise? Yes, the really interesting character wasn't the boy Luke, our cardboard cutout hero, but his immensely deeper, wiser and more evil father, Darth Vader. His story ends in redemption and death, but begs the question, how did he fall from grace and become a puppet in the hands of the Emperor Palpatine?

An excellent question that offers the opportunity to develop a work of great gravitas and tragic majesty, as the promising and noble Annikin Skywalker is seduced and betrayed into taking up the Dark Side and losing everything except the illusion of power. And you can see that George is trying. In the "reveal" at the end of the movie, Darth Vader is winched up before our eyes, like an important piece of scenery. The music swells to fever pitch, the dry ice is flowing, the lighting is perfect - surely a Titan or God is being born on the Grand Operatic Stage George Lucas believes he has created? Don Giovanni? Gotterdammerung?

Nope. Underneath the Dark Helmet, breathing stentoriously, is a puling, whining, ill-disciplined, complainer. A whingeing careerist who didn't get what he wanted when he wanted it and decided to take it out on everyone. In the first trilogy, Darth Vader had gravitas and a certain tragic nobility. Here, his precursor is a lightweight; nothing of note. His moral transformation is as slight as a breeze. The characterisation is so shallow as if to be almost non-existent. Lucas moves the characters about like plot-driven tokens on a Risk board. There is no emotional connection between the audience and his actors. He doesn't even attempt the barest minimum of emotional consistency within Skywalker's character. On one hand we are led to believe that he will embrace the Dark Side on the flimsy premise that he must do so to save Padme's life, on the other he is prepared to kill her on the most spurious misunderstanding, and without giving her the chance to explain. He rails against the Jedi Council for not awarding him the title of Master and in doing so, exemplifies why they would be stupid to do so.

In the end, all the basic plot points are covered so that the petty tyrants who require consistency in their fantasy timelines should be generally satisfied. The most obvious loose ends are tied up, and then some. Is it really credible, for example, that Princess Leia's distinctive "danish" hairstyle is something she would inherit from her dead mother? Extreme Lamarckism, I would have said. Did the one wookie mentioned by name really have to be Chewbacca? Are we really that dumb we have to led by the nose?

I saw the film with my 13 year-old nephew - surely within the target demographic that Lucas aims for. As soon as the film's opening action sequence ended and a turgid longeur of bad writing, bad direction, bad acting and tiresome plot exposition began, he dropped off for a nap until the light sabre action started again. Despite having a guaranteed audience of excited kids and nostalgic adults, it turns out that Lucas couldn't really hold our attention or deliver the goods. The original Darth Vader deserved so much more and Lucas delivered so much less.

Overcooked, overwrought and underwhelming.

title: Better than 1/2, worse than 4/5/6
review:
***Spoilers***

With the deluge of bad reviews that Lucas received from his first two efforts to reinstate the Star Wars franchise, Revenge of the Sith may have more aptly adopted Episode IV's moniker as it provided A New Hope for George. While he fails to deliver in a way that the 70's films did, he does provide a neat conclusion to the special effects marvel he begun with Episode I. We get Vader, we get twins, we get wookies. We do not however receive believable performances from the film's most important characters.

Hayden Christensen continues his dismal acting job as he draws us into the internal conflict that transforms playful Anakin Skywalker into the sinister Darth Vader. This is done through a collection of dream sequence premonitions that leave Anakin desperate to save his wife. As tensions pile up, Anakin questions his loyalties and begins his descent into the dark side. Unfortunately this is done far too abruptly. We are tossed about as Anakin moves from the verge of killing Palpatine to pledging his undying allegiance to him within seconds. This allegiance is apparently strong enough to drive him to murder innocent children in what seems like moments later. What kind of struggle is this? Continuing in this line, Anakin swears all he has done has been out of love, yet he attempts to kill poor Padmé shortly thereafter. What is his real motive, love or power? This could be neither or both, but Christensen fails to achieve even a remote sense of connectedness to this conflict. He comes off more like a brooding child than a deeply tortured adult. In the later films, Vader is always portrayed as calm, cool, and collected. There is no maturation in this film, however, and Anakin remains from beginning to end passionate and overly brash. This is culminated in an absurdly ridiculous "NOOOOOO" scream near the end of the movie after Vader puts on his suit for the first time. It would be laughable were it not making a complete mockery of one of the greatest villains of all time. Other notable failures include Samuel L. Jackson's portrayal as Mace Windu. The man mostly remembered as "baddest mother f---er" struggles desperately to pull off the role of a deeply contemplative monk fighter. It would have been nice to see a little more expression out of him, especially in his fight with Palpatine, but Jackson fails to connect.

This brings me to the saving grace of this film. Ian McDiarmid is fantastic as Palpatine. His performance conveys all the latent complexity, cleverness, and malevolence that Darth Sidious should rightly hold. Ewan McGregor does a pretty decent job as Obi Wan as well, and the final lightsaber battle between him and Vader is amazing.

Dialogue in this movie is generally poor especially in Yoda's case. After "Begun, the clone war has" I didn't think it could get much worse until I heard "Not if anything to say about it, I have". OK we get it, he says things in the wrong order. That is no excuse to drag in trite drivel to overemphasize the point. I also think CGI is overrated for characters. I miss the gritty realism of the muppets. And why Chewbacca? Wookies are cool, but this specific character inclusion only reduces the believability of the coincidences required to bring him back into the story later. Oh yeah, C3PO and R2D2 get memory wipes. "Oh Dear!" Convenient? A little too convenient, if you ask me.

All in all, it was good to see Lucas return to some of the splendor he enjoyed from his glory days. I don't think he ever really recovered from the terrible casting decision he made in Anakin, however(both child and adult). Awesome special effects, decent story, poor acting. 6 out of 10

title: Lucas is good in something, but it's definitely not writing and directing
review: Well, the expectations came to their and. A hell lot of money was spent on promoting, and The Revenge Of The Sith made a fortune for the producers. Therefore George Lucas has succeeded. Unfortunately the movie was week. The only two positive things I can mention without spoilers are the following: despite the duration of 2.5 hours, the movie is not a bit boring. And the other reveal: Jar-Jar gets only 4 seconds. They should have worked more on the script. The channel towards the "original trilogy" is incoherent, the dialogs are lame, and Yoda speaks an annoying English. (He always does, but this time he gets too many lines.) I see Hollywood on the downhill, because it's getting a more and more important aspect about scenes to "make the audience loving it" instead of "simply being good". So after killing the Matrix, the Star Wars galaxy ended up in the deep. Let's hope when some will decide to make another trilogy of this galaxy, it will be done by experts, not marketing people.

review: Better than I and II but original is the best. Sure, the visual effects is stunning.Don't blink or u'll miss. But the storyline is still incomparable with the original movies. call me old-fashioned but i prefer the set atmosphere. the movie is certainly very good action-wise, with edge of your seat thrilling title: The best of a bad bunch, but just too contrived
review: OK, it's better than the woeful part 1 and the mind numbing part 2, but lets be honest that's not exactly hard! Visually stunning this film falls down in too many ways to be a classic. Firstly the dialog's, clunky, too many one liners delivered by actors who; either know they are too good for it (Ewan McGregor, Natalie Portman, Samuel L Jackson) or would find it hard to act their way out of a paper bag (Hayden Christensen). Only Ian McDiarmid has any decent script to play with and he does it beautifully. Unfortunately he is playing opposite the wooden Christnesen for most of it!! Secondly, we all know what's going to happen, in part 4 so we know that Obi Wan, Yoda, Vader and the Emperor wont die, and just about everyone else will. There are no surprises and as a result very little tension in the second half of the film. My biggest problem with the film is the turning to the dark side of Anakin. It happens so fast, one minute he loves his wife the next he's butchering "Younglings" it really doesn't flow. I think this probably stems from the actors lack of visible talent. I was delighted when the mask finally goes on and we get the beautiful tones of James Earl Jones instead. So I give it a 6, mostly for the visuals, stunning fights and because Jar Jar isn't in it!! I still feel that the world would have been just as good a place with only the original 3 films, which were all so much better that this.

title: So Much Potential
review:
This movie blew away the first two, no question about that. I also greatly enjoyed it.

However, this movie had SOOOOO much potential. Yet it failed in several categories.

Special FX: Simply amazing, nothing to say about this, most likely the best star wars movie in this category (which is logical since it's the most recent) Plot Line: The basic plot line of this movie is amazing, any star wars fan would agree. I even have to go as far as saying that the plot line makes it a pretty foolproof movie. It was almost impossible to make this movie completely flop because the story line is so good.

Acting: OMG!!!!!! Why was the acting sooooo bad!?! Was there only one take per scene or something???? Hayden Christensen was horrible....it was disgusting! Several "dramatic" dialogs btw he and Natalie Portman actually made me laugh......I mean did they prepare for this movie by watching soap operas? This movie had such dramatic potential..... Anakin Skywalker becoming "evil" because he wanted to do "good." The total destruction of the Jedis. Ewan McGregor had so much more charisma than Christensen, yet some of his character was ruined by plain bad lines.

I feel like two main things stopped this movie from perfection. The first is the acting. The second is the directing. The most important part of the movie, Skywalker turning bad and killing off the Jedis, and the clones killing the Jedis, felt really compressed. It happened in like ten minutes. It's like, he's good, oh there he goes murdering children. What???? I think the main problem goes further back, to the first two movies. Why was the phantom menace so bad? The phantom menace and the aotc could have been compressed. I even remember talking to a friend about a month ago and saying...it's gonna be tough for them to go from AOTC to a new hope in just one movie. Or they could have made the movie three hours long. I think if Lucas had really cared about his movies, he would have done that. Honestly I think he is just a money making machine without a soul.

Also many of the references to the original movies and some of the tie ins felt a little forced. Like Lucas knew that he had to put them in but he didn't want to think about it too much so he just randomly threw them in. A few scenes mimicked scenes from the original three, a few lines were references, that remained subtle and was OK. But some of the stuff was just bam in you face! I also thought giving R2-D2 all these new powers was a bit overkill! And the part about erasing C3PO's memory bank, such a cheap way out.

Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed this movie. But as I was exiting the theaters, I reflected back on the new trilogy as a whole. When it comes down to it, Lucas had, in practice, an infinite budget for these films. He could have done anything he wanted to, could have taken all the time he needed, gotten pretty much any actor he wanted. He basically had total creative control of the project. Considering those things, I think he really blew it. This greatly angers the Star Wars fan inside me. I feel like I've been used, milked for my money and not given something in return. There are so many loyal star wars fans out there that have made Lucas both a Legend and an extremely rich man. And this is how he repays them.

When I see Peter Jackson, I see a genius. What he was able to do with LOTR is simply amazing, and is born from a passion to really translate Tolkein's work in the best way possible. When I look at Lucas I see an imbecile, only out there to make money. Not really caring about either his fan base or the artistic values of his film. Thanks George!

title: The Force is strong, but Lucas lost the plot...
review:
Minor Spoilers contained. (Are there any 'spoilers' left in this movie?!) No doubt 'Revenge of the Sith' will do phenomenally well at the box office. There surely aren't many people, who are even remotely interested in movies, who will want to miss out on not only the missing link in one of the most successful and popular movie franchises of all time, but also the chance to see the on-screen ascension (or rather, descension) of possibly the most iconic villain in movie history.

So you could say that George Lucas has his work cut out for him. (under statement of the year?!) So, has Lucas succeeded in making a masterpiece that far surpasses the mediocrity of Episodes 1 & 2 and justifies the gaps between the 2 sagas? Honestly, I wish I could say that he has, but he has left me feeling disappointed and wanting more.

Now, let me say first of all that I really enjoyed Episode 3. When all is said and done, my opinion of this movie is that it is great. The action far eclipses anything that has been seen in any of the star wars films to date, and on the one hand, that for me is the biggest attraction; seeing Jedi like Obi-Wan, Anakin and Yoda involved in some hot lightsabre action. For this reason, you will forgive Episode 3 a lot.

The film also has what episodes 1 & 2 seemed to lack a lot of, which is heart. There is a strong emotional core to this film, which is imperative given the subject matter, that makes for ultimately great viewing. There are also some marvellous performances, specifically Ian McDiarmid's brilliant Palpatine/Darth Sidious and Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi.

Where I feel 'Sith' really suffers, however, is in the brain department. Quite aside from some extremely ropey dialogue (something of a Lucas trademark it seems, having watched Episode 1 & 2 recently!) there are also some gaping plot holes and a severe lack of valuable character exposition, namely in Anakin. Here we have a Jedi, albeit tormented by his pride and his desire to save his wife Padme, but a Jedi nonetheless who turns to the dark side in the space of 5 seconds. Here was I expecting to see a great narrative driven piece showing an actual struggle between Anakin and his conscience. No, what we get instead is Anakin holding a lightsabre to Palpatine's throat and turning him in to the Jedi council one minute, and almost the very next frame he is kneeling before him, calling him master, before going off to mindlessly slaughter Jedi children with nary a decent explanation of why. Even Anakin's stunned realisation, "What have I done", that comes after seeing Palpatine dispose of Mace Windu, goes totally unanswered.

In another moment, one of the film's finer action sequences, we see Yoda facing off against Darth Sidious, the two real titanic powers on each side of the force. After matching one another blow for force-fuelled blow, we see something that just seems downright stupid. Yoda running away. Sure, he's small, but this little green guy is supposed to kick ass! Here is the most powerful Jedi in the galaxy, supposedly fighting for all he believes in, to save the Jedi order, yet after a little scuffle which he doesn't even lose, he turns around talking about "into exile I must go".

It seems to me that the prequel trilogy's failings reside chiefly in Lucas's determination to tie every minute detail together, and his inability to do so satisfactorily. The result of this is that he makes the world which he created all the more smaller, instead of highlighting what should be the expanse of his imagination.

I want to finish by adding a final criticism of Lucas, which is simply to compare Lucas' Jedi to Genndy Tartakovsky's, the man who co-wrote and directed the Clone Wars animated series which chronicles the events in between Episode's 2 and 3. Anyone who has seen the series should agree that Tartakovsky's Jedi are far more exciting, original and generally more awesome than Lucas's! It seems to me, when you compare the films to the series, that Tartakovsky has truly realised the potential of what Jedi can accomplish and created some truly astonishing action sequences from it. It is almost upsetting to see that Lucas, the man who blessed the world with the concept of the Force and the idea of Jedi, has been unable to demonstrate the depth of that power in the same way that Tartakovsky does. Although I fully appreciate that Star Wars is entirely Lucas's creation, I for one would love to see more of Tartakovsky's Star Wars and less of Lucas'. At least until he learns to write a decent script and learns to cut out the annoying 'wipe-fade' crap!! 8 for Jedi + 7 for Yoda kicking ass + 9 for Palpatine + 10 for Vader's first breath(!) - 9 for rubbish dialogue - 9 for Anakin's 'transformation' - 9 for Lucas letting me down when it could have been so much more...

7/10

review:

title: Very good, could be better
review:
Visually stunning. I'm not one to rave about the special effects, but the overall appearance of the movie is fantastic.

Excellent story line. There were also a lot of loose ends that had do be tied here, and they were tied up in a satisfying manner, while presenting a story that could stand on its own legs as a compelling adventure.

Sadly, however, they seem to have left the details of the writing to the summer interns. The dialogue is flat, predictable, and uninspiring. It says what is obviously occurring on the screen. Example (to avoid a spoiler), late in the film character x gets off the ship and really needs to go to the y, quickly, and someones says, "Take x to the y, quickly!" Gag! Even Padme's big scene, something that they should have worked hard on if for no other reason than to put it in the trailer to bring in the chicks, is spoiled by corny lines.

Carrie Fischer complained about some of the dialogue in the first (or fourth movie, if you reckon it that way), but, "Governor Tarkin. I should have expected to find you holding Vader's leash. I detected your foul stench when I was brought on board." is probably better than the best line in ROTS.

title: Revenge of the Theatre Seats
review:
30 minutes into this film I found myself thinking that I'll have a really exciting review to pass onto friends. "The new Star Wars has the best effects yet!" And that is where the excitement ended.

More than 1.5 hours later after many in the audience had left the theater early - a new low for Lucas films - I joined the audience in stumbling towards the exits with numb back and legs, wondering how this movie could "only be", two hours and ten minutes long!

Without a doubt the film series that gave birth to so many aspects of present day special effects technology had to top everything that came in the wake of its 3-decade legacy, just to make the grade. And this movie does break new ground in spacial effects realism. In a good cinema the opening scenes will have some viewers grappling with aerial-spacial phobias.

That said, Lucas must have invested in 'name' actors to sell the film, because the talent of some of the best and brightest names in the industry never makes it to the screen. There is precious little dialogue, and all of it is delivered with less emotion than a weather forecast. Some of the more intimate and human interactive scenes are shot in profile or behind the speakers. So after lousy script and pitiful acting, anything the high-paid talent might add to the scene with facial expressions, was left on the cutting room floor.

And where is the humor that characterized the earlier Star Wars flics? There is not a witty line, not even a humorous corny line, nor comedy scene in the film.

What's left? Action, effects, and plot line? Yeah. The audience is whalloped with wave after wave of action scenes, all shot in dreary lighting to make sure that no one forgets that this is the serious Star Wars flic. Most of these scenes could have been edited for impact.

OVERALL EFFECT ON THE AUDIENCE: special effects = 9, good action sequences = 8, plot = 6, visually confusing, excessively loud action sequences = -5, excessive number of loud action action sequences = -5, intelligence-insulting dialogue = -3, lack of acting = -4 TOTAL = 6

title: The best of the prequels, but still incomplete & lacking in parts
review: In Episode III, George Lucas obviously has changed his game plan, and improved enormously from the wreck that Episode's I & II were. He still fails to recapture what he had 25 years ago, but this is definitely not a complete failure. It succeeds in filling most gaps, and finally adding some emotion and character development, and definitely is entertaining. Where Lucas fails, unfortunately is in some of the most important parts, which definitely effects the film as a whole, which is disappointing. ***SPOILERS*** ************** The biggest problem occurs halfway through the film, where Anakin fatefully turns to the dark side. Until this point, the film was doing very well portraying in a somewhat realistic way, exactly how Anakin started to fall. But then it drops. In one sequence with very little dialogue, Anakin betrays everything he has been trained to believe, commits himself to the emperor, and becomes Darth Vader. This was a surprise, since in the scene preceding it, he is sick to almost the point of vomiting, once finding out the emperor is evil, and tells Mace Windu this, so that the emperor can be brought down. This is the largest failing point. The ending was also equally unsatisfying, surprisingly when the suit is put on, and Darth Vader says only 2 words which the Darth Vader we know would actually say. After they are spoken unfortunately, he continues talking like the whiny Anakin from Episode II, which left me upset. So those are the two largest pitfalls the movie suffers. ***END OF SPOILERS*** ********************* In whole, the film is a success, and definitely the best of the new trilogy, but it still definitely does not measure to the originals, but is still as I said a success, and worth your time.

title: Parts better than the whole
review:
The beginning battle and fights scenes are good. But the first third of the film up until the first act turning point is weak and closer to Episode II or I. After that when Anakin begins to 'turn' it starts to get good. However, the stronger tragic parts (where I actually felt some swelling of real emotion for the first time in these new episodes) are let down by the weaker parts. Plus, the ending doesn't feel conclusive enough - the film just ends. Empire manages to avoid this problem by building up to the conclusion better but still leaving just enough pieces hanging and unanswered questions (such as is Darth Vader 'really' Luke's father? and how will they rescue Han Solo and the love story turn out?).

POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD!

I guess the main problem is here is we already know all the rest. If Lucas was a better writer he could have utilized the elements of Greek tragedy better, rather than make Darth Vader's last cry so cartoonish: NOOOOOOOOOOOO!!!!! But most of all, the contradictions of these new installments just gets too much to enable them to be integrated with the older ones without having to dramatically cut out bits in one or the other trilogies. First the force is more spiritual - 'zen' like, then it's biological things in our blood. The stormtroopers have normal accents, and then we're supposed to believe their all clones with Maori voices (Not to mention Bobba Fett!). Plus the messages are a tad preachy and didactic in these films compared to the others, regarding tyranny versus democracy. Plus Darth Sidious could have had a much better argument - perhaps a rhetorical speech rather than - LETS BE AN EMPIRE! REPLY: YEAH!!

There are others problems..with Chewie and C-3P0 and R2D2 and the problem of trying to tie bits together that don't work, but the most standout one is: In Return of the Jedi Luke asks Leia are in the Ewok village, and Luke asks her if she remembers her mother, her 'real mother'. Yes she does, she remembers little things about, that 'she was very kind and very sad'. With the tragic turn of events at the end of Revenge of the Sith it is not possible for Leia to have this memory. Rationalise it anyway you want to, but the fact is Lucas may have created Star Wars, but that doesn't mean if he chooses to change the originals by changing their past that overall things will be necessarily better. I prefer the original installments, and believe that without Episodes I through III, they are better films.

title: Not bad for an action movie (might contain spoilers)
review:

title: The turn to the Dark Side is not believable
review:
***Some mild spoilers***

I must say that I have mixed feelings for the movie. The movie is "ok" and fully watchable (and even enjoyable), but I am not really sure it's better than 'Attack Of The Clones' (however I like it better than 'Return of the Jedi' which I never particularly liked -- too isolated of an incident for my taste).

The motivations turning Anakin to the dark side are just not convincing. What Lucas should have done is place Amidala in danger while in a diplomatic mission, have the Jedis accompanying her fail to rescue her because she was not the priority of the mission, have Amidala give birth and die in the mission, and then have Anakin go berserk over the Jedi and turn against them while joining the Sith. THIS is something that can turn a man in love in to a lunatic, and THIS human nature is what Lucas should have exploited to make the turn to the Dark Side believable.

Only a fool would have fallen for the reasons Anakin fell for. And if Star Wars is just the family story of a fool, then we better not watch in the first place.

As for Padme's death, this was unconvincing too. I know a species of fish that die in that way, but I never seen or heard of a human. :P

Some scenes are cheesy and unnecessary and others they could have been done better if Hayden Christiansen had a bit of *imagination* on how to act with more passion. The guy seems to lack the imagination required to construct situations in his head so he can act on them more naturally. He is *better* than in AOTC, but still worse than any other actor in the movie.

Personally, I liked the character of Senator Bail Organa. He was the real deal, somehow.

Overall: 7/10

title: Bad Acting, Bad Dialogue, but entertaining
review: I'm not nitpicking when i say that i can't take hayden seriously as darth vader. His voice is still too soft and his anger is never really convincing. His constant glowering is also rather annoying. Padme, once a brave and determined senator and queen, has for some reason or another been reduced to that of some fearful woman who cant help herself. The only good acting was done by the chancellor himself, actually, very good now that i remember. This isn't intended to be an essay on the movie, so basically...Yes, it tied up loose ends and connected 3 to 4. Yes, there were awesome fight scenes. Yes, the plot is generally interesting, And yes, it was overall better than 1 and 2. But the poor dialogue remains and the casting of some west coast underwear model type of guy will forever tarnish what this movie could have accomplished in its search for redemption on the last two. Wasn't a bad movie, but it simply wasn't going to be one that is going to be remembered. Maybe my expectations were too high being a respectful fan of the trilogy. I however, believe the rating shouldn't be as good as what is being given right now..(8.2). IT's exactly like how ROTK is rated higher than the first two, even though the third one was arguably the worst of the three...interesting

title: Birth of the Empire
review: Just saw the movie this weekend and it's excellent for its genre. The thread in the plot where Anakin is lured by the dark side and turns into the evil George Bush is quite compelling. Kind of puts the other movies into context, like the "Attack Of The Clones", the exception being that the feeble minded clones are not controlled by blind religious fervor and unquestionable obedience to their masters/makers, only the latter is needed for the movie version. And so the birth of the Empire commences.

title: my personal review
review:
After viewing the latest and final installment of the Star Wars saga, The Revenge of the Sith I found myself contemplating what I actually thought of the film. I have come to a number of conclusions, both good and bad. First, from an entertainment perspective, I found the film to be really enjoyable. By far, the action and fight sequences were better than episode one and two. The film did also answer some of my burning questions as to why certain things happened in the original series.

Now on to the negative aspects of the film. My biggest beef was the fact that Anakin's turnover to the dark side was very sudden. I felt that Lucas should have depicted more raw emotion other than the occasional tear from Anakin. I felt that he did not contemplate his decisions, he just decided to turn once he said "what have I done" in response to Mace Windu's death.

I also found Padme's death unnecessary. Although Anakin does have a premonition, I found that the "lost the will to live" aspect quite dumb. Why did she lose the will to live when she knew Anakin still had good left in him. Upon discovering the passing of Padme, Darth Vader does the worst "nooo" in the history of Star Wars. I found that to be unnecessary and he should have depicted more emotion. To me, he turned to the dark side for nothing because Padme died anyways despite his effort to save her from death. So what now? Something should have been said about that.

I enjoyed the parallelism between Yoda and Sidious and Obi-Wan and Darth Vader's fights. I also liked the parallel between the birth of Luke and Leia and the transformation of Darth Vader unsuited to Darth Vader suited.

Overall I enjoyed the episode and I am sad to see the saga come to an end. I can't believe after almost 30 years it is all over.

title: Nice Try But No Brass Ring
review:
After the heated opening and things settle down from all the hoop-la even sane Star Wars addicts will admit that the acting & dialog were painful to endure. Too bad, 'cause the visual fireworks were great. Lucas? If your listening....Go back and watch your own original #4. There the characters were fun and their interaction was great. We bonded with each and every one. Carrie Fisher, Harrison Ford, Mark Hammel, and most of all Sir Alec Guiness made the magic happen. I guess it's the IL' story of seeing the forest for the trees.

All in all it still was a wild ride with all the FX and computer wizardry. Gee if only we saw what could have been.

title: Otherworldly
review:
Star Wars: Episode III--Revenge of the Sith Grade: A Director: George Lucas Screenplay: Lucas Cast: Ewan McGregor (Moulin Rouge), Natalie Portman (Closer), Hayden Christensen (Shattered Glass) Rating: PG John DeSando, WCBE's "It's Movie Time"

The Force in contemporary popular film criticism comes from the New York Times, so when critic A.O. Scott weighs in on George Lucas's Star Wars: Episode III--Revenge of the Sith, I listen: "This is by far the best film in the more recent trilogy, and also the best of the four episodes Mr. Lucas has directed. That's right (and my inner 11-year-old shudders as I type this): it's better than 'Star Wars.' "

With so many reviews echoing Scott, I will not repeat my similar praise but alter it slightly by saying that Sith is second for me to the original now called Episode IVA New Hope, which has a clarity, innocence, and spirit so reflective of my family and the time when we saw it I cannot allow any other episode to eclipse it. Sith may be superior, but my memory preserves the primacy of the first Star Wars. More interesting than my nostalgia is the allegorical commentary even Lucas admits is underneath Sith. When Darth Vader tells Obi-Wan, "If you're not with me, you're my enemy," no conscious adult can miss the echo of George Bush's similar challenge. Obi-Wan's response is a liberal's rejoinder to the 21st-century neocon's streamlined mantras: "Only a Sith thinks in absolutes."

Lucas himself, while admitting that he started this line of thinking about Nixon and Vietnam with the notion that "the senate could give itself over, could surrender to a dictator," said recently, "I hope that situation never arises in our country. Maybe the film will awaken people to this danger."

What makes Sith superior to all other sci-fi films, even others in its own canon, is the CGI that is itself otherworldly: The battle scenes are full of interstellar acrobatics with the usual ironic humor and the light saber fights so evocative of old-fashioned Errol Flynn/ Han Solo swashbuckling that the film carries itself to greatness on the tails of technology.

title: Excellent finish to a great series of movies!
review:
I loved this one. Episode I was fun because it was Star Wars again, but overall, I thought it was just OK. Too much JarJar and the business that Darth Vader built C3PO was just plain silly. Episode 2 was much better.

Episode 3 Ranked up there with the original 3 episodes (IV,V, and VI). I actually liked it better than VI (hated the teddy bear Ewoks and the dance party at the end).
